questions.q: m-Dinitrobenzene is treated with aqueous ammonium sulphide, (NH₄)₂S. The product is:
questions.explain: The Zinin reduction reduces only one of the two nitro groups, giving m-nitroaniline (3-nitroaniline). Both groups would be reduced to m-phenylenediamine by Sn/HCl, Fe/HCl or catalytic hydrogenation.

questions.q: Which reagent reduces only ONE nitro group of m-dinitrobenzene?
questions.explain: Sulphide reagents (Na₂S, NaSH, NH₄SH, (NH₄)₂S) are mild and give selective reduction. Metal–acid and catalytic hydrogenation reduce every nitro group present.

questions.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol is treated with sodium sulphide. The product is:
questions.explain: Sodium sulphide reduces 2,4-dinitrophenol selectively to 2-amino-4-nitrophenol, leaving the second nitro group in place. A diamine would need metal–acid reduction, and the OH group is not replaced.

questions.q: The usual explanation for why Zinin reduction stops after one nitro group is reduced is that:
options: Sulphide is consumed completely after one nitro group
The –NH₂ group formed makes the ring richer in electrons, so the remaining –NO₂ is reduced much more slowly
The second nitro group is converted into a diazonium salt
The product precipitates as a sulphide salt
questions.explain: Sulphide is a weak reductant, and once the first –NO₂ becomes electron-donating –NH₂ the second nitro group is less electron-poor and reacts far more slowly. The reaction can therefore be stopped at the nitroaniline.
